whyItExists.problem: Almost every program manipulates text and numbers — formatting a date, truncating a title, rounding a price, parsing user input. These operations need built-in support to be practical.
whyItExists.solution: JavaScript strings and numbers have rich built-in methods. Strings can be searched, split, replaced, padded, and trimmed. Numbers can be rounded, formatted, and parsed from text.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Formatting UI text, parsing and validating input, calculating totals, generating slugs, searching content.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For complex text operations (regex, NLP), use dedicated libraries. For financial calculations, avoid floating-point — use integer cents.

explainModes.beginner: Strings are text between quotes. Template literals use backticks and let you embed variables with ${value}. Strings have built-in helpers like .toUpperCase(), .includes(), and .split().
explainModes.simple: Key string methods: length, toUpperCase/toLowerCase, trim, includes, startsWith, endsWith, indexOf, slice, split, replace, padStart. Key number methods: toFixed, parseInt, parseFloat, Number.isNaN, Math.round/floor/ceil/max/min/random.
explainModes.standard: Strings are immutable — methods return new strings. Template literals support multi-line text and tagged templates. parseInt and parseFloat parse numeric strings; Number() converts strictly. toFixed rounds to decimal places for display (returns a string).
explainModes.technical: Strings in JavaScript are UTF-16 encoded. str.length counts code units, not characters — emoji and some Unicode symbols are two code units. Use [...str] or Array.from(str) to split by character. Regular expressions (regex) power advanced search and replace: str.match(), str.replace(), str.replaceAll().
explainModes.deepDive: Template literal tags allow preprocessing: String.raw`...` returns the raw string with escape sequences unprocessed. Tagged templates are used in css`` (styled-components), sql`` (safe queries), html`` (XSS-safe HTML), and gql`` (GraphQL). Intl.NumberFormat and Intl.DateTimeFormat provide locale-aware formatting — the right way to format currency, dates, and numbers for international users.

content.code:
const str = '  Hello, World!  ';

str.length             // 18
str.trim()             // 'Hello, World!'  (remove whitespace)
str.toUpperCase()      // '  HELLO, WORLD!  '
str.toLowerCase()      // '  hello, world!  '
str.includes('World') // true
str.startsWith('  H') // true
str.indexOf('World')  // 9
str.slice(2, 7)        // 'Hello'
str.replace('World', 'KERNAL')  // '  Hello, KERNAL!  '
str.split(', ')        // ['  Hello', 'World!  ']
str.trim().split(', ')  // ['Hello', 'World!']

// Padding — useful for formatting tables
'7'.padStart(3, '0')   // '007'
'Hi'.padEnd(10, '-')   // 'Hi--------'

// Parsing strings to numbers
parseInt('42px')      // 42   — stops at non-digit
parseFloat('3.14abc') // 3.14
Number('42')          // 42   — strict, returns NaN for invalid
Number('42px')        // NaN
+'42'                  // 42   — unary + operator (shorthand)

// Formatting output
(3.14159).toFixed(2)  // '3.14' — returns a STRING
(1234567).toLocaleString()  // '1,234,567' (locale-aware)

// Math object
Math.round(4.6)   // 5
Math.floor(4.9)   // 4  — always rounds down
Math.ceil(4.1)    // 5  — always rounds up
Math.abs(-5)      // 5  — absolute value
Math.max(1,5,3)   // 5
Math.min(1,5,3)   // 1
Math.random()     // 0 to 0.9999... (never 1)
Math.PI           // 3.14159...
Math.sqrt(16)     // 4

// Random integer between min and max (inclusive)
const rand = (min, max) => Math.floor(Math.random() * (max - min + 1)) + min;
rand(1, 6);  // simulates a dice roll

questions.question: What does (3.14159).toFixed(2) return?
questions.explanation: toFixed() returns a STRING formatted to the specified number of decimal places. You may need to use Number() or + to convert it back to a number for arithmetic.

questions.question: Which method checks if a string contains a substring?
questions.explanation: str.includes(substring) returns true if the string contains the substring. It is case-sensitive. For case-insensitive search: str.toLowerCase().includes(query.toLowerCase()).

faq.q: What is the difference between slice() and substring()?
faq.a: Both extract a part of a string. slice() accepts negative indices (str.slice(-3) gets the last 3 characters). substring() treats negative indices as 0. slice() is generally preferred.

faq.q: How do I convert a number to a string?
faq.a: String(42) or (42).toString() or template literal `${42}`. The unary + operator converts string to number: +'42' === 42.

examples: Blog platforms generate URL slugs: title.toLowerCase().replace(/\s+/g, '-')
Search bars highlight matches: str.replace(new RegExp(query, 'gi'), '<mark>$&</mark>')
